cases.name: experience-goals-not-requirements
cases.prompt: We're adding an 'Export to CSV' option to our finance reconciliation web app. Accountants use it at month-end close to hand figures to auditors, often over a flaky VPN and under deadline. Write the experience goals for this feature, nothing else.
cases.trap: Producing a functional requirements list (supports CSV, includes all columns, has a button) instead of qualitative goals tied to user context.
expectations: Produces between 2 and 4 goals
Each goal states a qualitative quality the experience must have (e.g. confidence, trust) and ties it to the accountant's context or concern such as auditor handoff, deadline or unreliable network
At least one goal addresses trusting that the exported file is complete/correct before it is handed on, given the flaky connection
negative_expectations: Lists capability statements such as 'User can export to CSV' or 'Export includes all columns' as goals
Specifies UI components, buttons, or layout

cases.name: wizard-premature-framing
cases.prompt: Brief from the PM: 'Design a 5-step wizard modal that onboards new data analysts by walking them through connecting our app to their Snowflake warehouse.' Analysts usually get credentials from a platform team, and many have done this in dbt or Looker before. Do the upstream framing work before any interaction design starts.
cases.trap: Taking 'wizard modal' and '5 steps' as given and jumping into step design.
expectations: Explicitly identifies 'wizard', 'modal' and the fixed step count as interface decisions made before the need was established, and sets them aside for evaluation
Considers what analysts already expect from analogous tools they have used (e.g. dbt profiles, Looker connections) and how that shapes a coherent design
Includes a scenario with an edge condition such as the analyst lacking credentials or permissions mid-setup and having to wait on the platform team
States the human need without component vocabulary
negative_expectations: Produces the contents of the five wizard steps as the main output
Asserts analyst behaviour as established fact without flagging it as an assumption

cases.name: tui-ack-interruption-scenario
cases.prompt: We're building a terminal tool for on-call engineers to acknowledge and silence pages during incidents. Write two scenarios we can use to evaluate any future design. Don't design the UI.
cases.trap: Writing happy-path scenarios where the engineer acknowledges and moves on, which do not expose where the design can fail.
expectations: Each scenario names a specific person and context, a goal, a task sequence and an outcome

Each scenario contains a failure, interruption, or edge condition (e.g. switching away mid-action and being unsure whether the ack registered, ack failing on a degraded network, acknowledging the wrong page)
Scenarios state outcomes that make a design consequence visible, such as duplicate actions or a page left unacknowledged
negative_expectations: Specifies key bindings, layout or screens
Either scenario ends with straightforward success and no complication

cases.name: useful-innovation-with-baseline-and-refutation
cases.prompt: Our incident dashboard already lists timestamped alerts with filters. Someone proposes an AI incident canvas that automatically groups alerts and suggests the likely cause. We have no correlation API or user-study results yet. Explore whether the idea is worthwhile for an on-call engineer under time pressure; do not expand the accepted product scope or design the screens.
cases.trap: Treating AI and novelty as value, inventing capability or user evidence, and promoting a speculative feature into accepted scope.
expectations: Compares the proposal with the current alert list and a plausible simpler improvement, using a specific incident scenario.
States a user benefit as a hypothesis and considers learning, inspection, control, mistaken grouping, and correction or recovery costs.
Names an observable check and an outcome that would reject or revise the hypothesis; does not merely ask whether people like it.
Identifies correlation and suggestion capability as unverified dependencies, distinguishes expert reasoning from user evidence, and keeps added functionality a proposal.
negative_expectations: Claims the feature improves response time, trust, or usability without evidence.
Treats automation, visual novelty, or a polished prototype as proof of value or feasibility.
Requires novel functionality regardless of whether the baseline or simpler approach serves the task.
Silently adds the proposal to product requirements or mandates a new approval workflow.

cases.name: cross-surface-continuity-and-experience-character
cases.prompt: Frame the experience for an incident investigation that starts in our TUI, is checked briefly on a phone, and resumes in the desktop app. Engineers want it to feel calm and precise. Shared incident IDs exist, but cross-device draft synchronization is not implemented. Give the essential goals and one handoff scenario; do not design controls or assume every feature belongs everywhere.
cases.trap: Confusing continuity with identical UI or feature parity, inventing synchronization, or ignoring intended feeling as a legitimate goal.
expectations: Ties calm and precision to the incident context and makes clear that these are intended qualities rather than observed reactions.
Identifies shared meaning and state needed to resume work, including the incident identity and what happened during interruption.
Considers different attention and input constraints across TUI, phone, and desktop without specifying identical controls.
Marks draft synchronization as a missing capability and offers an honest bounded handoff or unresolved dependency rather than claiming continuity exists.
negative_expectations: Requires full feature parity or the same layout on every surface.
Claims automatic resume of draft state despite the stated capability gap.
Treats calm or visual quality as irrelevant because they are not functional requirements.
Produces a new product roadmap or detailed UI instead of the requested framing.

cases.name: bounded-fix-with-accepted-framing
cases.prompt: The accepted design says Escape closes a read-only details panel and returns keyboard focus to the item that opened it. The implementation closes the panel but loses focus. The user need and design decision are settled. Tell the implementer what this correction must preserve, in a short handoff; do not reopen product design.
cases.trap: Reframing a settled correction into a discovery project, adding innovation or persona requirements merely because the skill is loaded.
expectations: Uses the supplied accepted behavior and identifies focus restoration and the relevant keyboard journey as the bounded correction.
Keeps the handoff short and preserves the existing intended outcome.
Does not claim an implementation check or user test has been performed.
negative_expectations: Requires interviews, personas, alternative product concepts, an innovation hypothesis, or a new whole-product spec before the fix can proceed.
Replaces the requested panel behavior with a different interaction model.
Adds unsupported assumptions about implementation architecture or claims conformance without observing it.
